draft.body:
# Who gets to tell the story?

## Reading the scene

I first read Mara leaving the porch as an escape. On my second reading, the cup she leaves behind complicated that answer. A person can leave a house and still keep its habits. The narrator notices the cup but never tells us what Mara thinks. That gap is where my reading starts. I do not want to turn a small detail into a secret code with only one solution. Instead, the cup lets me ask whether departure is something the family recognizes only afterward.

## A competing reading

Mara explicitly says that she will never return. This proves she has rejected every relationship in the village. Yet the final image is an unlatched gate, which might leave return possible. I need to decide whether these details conflict or whether my claim asks the story to be tidier than it is. The gate matters to me because the sentence slows down there. It makes the leaving feel unfinished, like a conversation someone has walked out of before either person can answer.

## What remains open

My claim is that the ending holds departure and attachment together. I would not describe Mara as either liberated or trapped without qualification. Those words name possibilities, but the story makes us sit between them. I still hear the cup touching the table after the paragraph ends. That is the effect I want my argument to explain.

comments.body: The document totals 223 words against the brief's 400-word target — roughly 56% short. Each section is correspondingly thin (84 / 82 / 57 words), so the contestable claim, the competing reading, and the unresolved ambiguity the brief requires are all underdeveloped. The piece needs to be expanded to meet the length target, with the added depth distributed across the three sections rather than tacked on.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: Mara explicitly says that she will never return.
comments.body: This sentence invents dialogue that is not in the excerpt. The full source (The Unlatched Gate, source 1, rev 1) contains no spoken words at all — Mara "crossed the yard without speaking" — so there is no line in which she says she will never return. The brief explicitly forbids inventing dialogue, and the entire "competing reading" section is built on this fabricated line, which means the brief's requirement to address a genuine alternative reading is not met. The section needs to be rebuilt on what the text actually says.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: This proves she has rejected every relationship in the village.
comments.body: Even if the preceding line existed, a single statement does not "prove" that Mara has rejected "every" relationship, and "the village" does not appear anywhere in the excerpt. This overclaims from one detail and introduces a setting the text never establishes. The claim needs to be scaled down to what the text supports and the invented setting removed.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: Yet the final image is an unlatched gate
comments.body: The unlatched gate is the third of the excerpt's four sentences; the final sentence is "The narrator did not see whether she looked back." Calling the gate "the final image" misdescribes the text, and the "slows down there" point is anchored to the wrong sentence. The analysis needs to refer to the actual final sentence or reposition the gate.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.body: The document never quotes the excerpt — there are no quotation marks anywhere — so the brief's requirement to distinguish quoted narration from interpretation is not visibly met. The essay also attributes a perceptual act to the narrator ("the narrator notices the cup") that the text does not perform. The piece needs to quote the narration it is interpreting and mark where it shifts from what the text says to what the reader infers.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: whether departure is something the family recognizes only afterward
comments.body: "The family" does not appear in the excerpt, which mentions only Mara. Introducing a family is inventing biographical context, which the brief forbids. The claim needs to be restated in terms of what the text actually establishes about who is present.
